analysis.one_liner: Exempts private agreements and cooperation from federal antitrust and unfair-competition laws.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have exempted private agreements from federal antitrust law, died in the Senate Judiciary Committee without a single cosponsor, a vote, or any further action.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite federal antitrust law so that no voluntary agreement, contract, or cooperation among individuals or groups of individuals could be prosecuted as an antitrust violation [S3]. In practice, that would immunize price-fixing cartels, market-splitting deals, and employer collusion — arrangements that are among the main things antitrust law exists to stop. Because corporations and business owners are groups of individuals, the exemption would cover business conduct, not just personal activity. The bill never advanced: it was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee and died there when the Congress ended [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Businesses that want to coordinate on prices, divide markets, or agree with competitors — conduct currently illegal under the Sherman and Clayton Acts — would gain immunity from federal antitrust prosecution [S3]. Large firms with market power would benefit most, since they are best positioned to profit from collusion.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Companies seeking to collude on prices

how_it_helps.text: It exempts voluntary economic coordination, cooperation, contracts, and covenants from the Sherman Act, the Clayton Act, and section 5 of the FTC Act [S3].

This would shield private agreements, including agreements among businesses and their owners, from antitrust prosecution, letting firms coordinate on prices, output, markets, or hiring without federal antitrust liability [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Consumers would pay the cost through higher prices, since collusion and price-fixing would no longer be illegal. Workers could pay through employer agreements that suppress wages, which are also currently actionable under antitrust law [S3].

drawbacks.text: Exempting voluntary agreements from the Sherman and Clayton Acts would legalize cartels, price-fixing, and market division among firms, directly raising prices for consumers.
Agreements among employers to hold down wages would fall under the exemption, hurting workers even though the bill's language mentions 'individuals' broadly.
The FTC's authority to police unfair competition would no longer reach voluntary coordination, weakening the government's main consumer-protection tool against mergers and collusion.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's stated aim was freedom from state interference in private agreements, but the main real-world effect would have been to let dominant companies fix prices, divide markets, and suppress wages without legal consequence. Congress's antitrust laws are the main check on concentrated corporate power over what consumers pay and what workers earn, and this would have removed that check broadly. There was no meaningful upside for consumers; even defenders of economic liberty generally accept that price-fixing harms the very markets the bill's supporters say they want to protect.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and died there when the Congress ended, with no cosponsors and no committee or floor vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on September 27, 2022 and read twice, then referred to the Committee on the Judiciary [S5].
No further action was taken before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, so the bill never received a committee markup or a floor vote [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Antitrust law remained intact, preserving legal protection against cartels, price-fixing, and employer collusion for consumers and workers. No industry gained the exemption it sought, because the bill never advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Consumers and workers; antitrust law survived

for.name: Sen. Rand Paul
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to exempt voluntary economic agreements from federal antitrust law.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; it never received a markup or vote.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Republican sponsor and no cosponsors from either party, so no party bloc took a position on it.

industries.note: The bill would exempt agreements among groups of individuals — which include corporations — from all federal antitrust law, allowing price-fixing and collusion among dominant firms [S3]. Consumers would bear the cost in higher prices and less competition.

industries.industry: Antitrust plaintiffs' lawyers and state antitrust enforcers
industries.note: Federal antitrust enforcement under the Sherman and Clayton Acts and FTC Act section 5 would no longer reach voluntary agreements, sharply shrinking the enforcement and litigation field [S3].
With collusion no longer illegal, buyers would face less competition and higher prices; antitrust law is the main legal protection against price-fixing [S3].
